implementation_notes: io-ts makes the two directions one value: a codec Type<A, O, I> decodes untrusted input into the static type A and encodes A back into its output type, so schema, validator and serializer are the same object and neither the domain type nor the wire format knows the other. zod follows the same shape with schema.parse plus an explicit serializer, and class-transformer drives both directions from decorators. The zero-dependency realization is a pair of pure functions (toWire/fromWire) plus a schema for the untrusted direction, because TypeScript types vanish at runtime; a converter class is needed only when conversions must be looked up dynamically by name.
pitfalls: encode does not validate: encoding a structurally wrong object produces a wrong payload silently, so round-trip tests are the only safety net.
Type declarations are erased at runtime, so a cast (as Ticket) at the boundary skips the codec; untrusted input must enter through decode(u: unknown).
A hand-written interface that shadows the codec's TypeOf drifts from the schema without a compile error.

variants.name: class-transformer plainToInstance/instanceToPlain with @Transform
variants.implementation_notes: The decorator-driven realization common in NestJS-style codebases: @Expose/@Exclude/@Type/@Transform mark how each field maps, and the two entry points plainToInstance (plain object to class instance) and instanceToPlain (instance to plain object) apply the same metadata in both directions, so the class carries the mapping and no separate converter object is written. Pair it with class-validator or a schema library for untrusted input, because the decorators convert without validating.
pitfalls: Without excludeExtraneousValues, unknown properties of the plain object are copied onto the instance, which is how untrusted payloads leak into typed objects.
The library converts but does not validate: a missing required property leaves undefined in a non-optional field.
Decorators need experimentalDecorators/emitDecoratorMetadata and a class value at runtime, so a type-only import silently loses the mapping.
Transform functions must stay pure and total; a throwing transformer aborts the whole conversion.
